aum.title: Assets under management
aum.content:
Total AUM is client assets BlackRock manages at period end; average AUM is the balance fee revenue is actually calculated on, since base fees accrue daily; long-term AUM excludes cash management (money-market) assets, which carry much lower fees.

For BlackRock, Inc.: AUM moves with markets (beta BlackRock does not control) and with net flows (BlackRock's own distribution performance) -- the net inflows chart below isolates the second.

What to watch:

  • Average AUM growth versus base fee growth (fee-rate/mix drift)
  • Gap between total and average AUM in a volatile quarter -- a market swing late in the quarter barely touches average, but will show up next quarter's fees

aumMix.title: AUM by asset class and vehicle
aumMix.content:
AUM split by asset class (equity, fixed income, multi-asset, private markets/alternatives, cash management) and, overlaid, by iShares ETF AUM -- a distribution vehicle that cuts across the equity and fixed-income classes rather than a class of its own.

For BlackRock, Inc.: private markets/alternatives AUM is the smallest slice but the highest fee rate and the growth priority after the GIP, HPS and Preqin deals; management targets technology and private markets combined at 30%+ of firm revenue by 2030.

What to watch:

  • Private markets AUM growth rate versus the rest of the mix
  • Equity AUM's sensitivity to market levels versus fixed income's relative stability

netInflows.title: Net inflows
netInflows.content:
Net inflows is new client money in less redemptions in the period, for total AUM, the long-term subset (ex cash management) and iShares ETFs specifically.

For BlackRock, Inc.: flows are the organic growth lever management is actually judged on each quarter -- unlike market appreciation, they are BlackRock winning (or losing) share. iShares ETF flows have been the largest and steadiest contributor in recent years.

What to watch:

  • Long-term flows as an annualised % of beginning long-term AUM (the organic growth rate management quotes)
  • Concentration in one or two large institutional mandates versus broad-based retail/ETF flows

fees.title: Base fees, performance fees and technology revenue
fees.content:
Base fees are the recurring advisory/administration fees on AUM and are the large majority of revenue; performance fees are incentive fees on alternatives/private markets funds that beat a hurdle, and are lumpy by design; technology services revenue (Aladdin and, after the Preqin deal, eFront/private-markets data) is a subscription-style ACV business management is growing deliberately faster than AUM-linked fees.

For BlackRock, Inc.: the mix shift toward performance fees and technology revenue is margin-accretive versus base fees alone, and is the basis for the 30%-of-revenue-by-2030 target for technology + private markets combined.

What to watch:

  • Performance fees as a share of revenue in a strong markets year -- not a reliable run-rate
  • Technology services revenue growth rate (double digits is the bar management has set)

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For BlackRock, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For BlackRock, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For BlackRock, Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For BlackRock, Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For BlackRock, Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax. Underlying operating margin is management's own as-adjusted measure, which strips deal costs, amortization of intangibles from acquisitions and other one-offs that GAAP operating margin cannot.

For BlackRock, Inc.: GAAP operating margin has been depressed by integration costs and intangible amortization from the GIP/HPS/Preqin deals; the underlying measure is the one management targets and the one comparable across quarters with different deal activity.

What to watch:

  • Underlying margin trend versus GAAP margin -- a widening gap means acquisition-related costs are growing
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For BlackRock, Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For BlackRock, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For BlackRock, Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For BlackRock, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
